clinicalPearls: Loss of eyelashes, and sometimes eyebrows, which is a sign rather than a disease in itself
Causes are broad: local lid disease, dermatological conditions, systemic disease, drugs, trauma and psychiatric causes
Chronic blepharitis is a common local cause, while alopecia areata and cicatricial alopecias affect the follicles
Loss of the lateral third of the eyebrows is a classic sign of hypothyroidism and of leprosy
Trichotillomania and factitious causes should be considered, especially with irregular patchy loss
A lid margin lesion with associated madarosis raises concern for eyelid malignancy
reference.pathophysiology: Madarosis results from any process that damages or destroys the eyelash (and eyebrow) follicles or disrupts the hair cycle. Non-scarring loss occurs with conditions such as alopecia areata, telogen effluvium, hypothyroidism and drug effects, where follicles are preserved and regrowth is possible. Scarring (cicatricial) loss follows chronic inflammation, cicatrising skin disease or infiltrating eyelid tumours that destroy the follicles, causing permanent loss. Identifying whether the loss is scarring or non-scarring guides the search for cause and the likelihood of regrowth.
additionalDifferentials: Eyelid malignancy (for example basal or sebaceous cell carcinoma)
additionalInvestigations: Examination of the lid margin, skin and pattern of hair loss
Assessment for scarring versus non-scarring loss
Biopsy of any suspicious lid margin lesion
Investigation for systemic or dermatological causes as directed by the history
redFlags: A localised lid margin lesion with lash loss suggesting malignancy
Systemic features suggesting endocrine or infiltrative disease
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the cause: non-scarring loss often recovers when the underlying condition is treated, whereas scarring loss and tumour-related loss are permanent.
pitfalls: Overlooking an eyelid malignancy causing localised lash loss
Missing hypothyroidism with lateral eyebrow loss
Not distinguishing scarring from non-scarring loss
management: Treat the identified underlying cause, since madarosis is a sign rather than a disease in itself
Manage local lid disease, especially chronic blepharitis, with lid hygiene, warm compresses and topical or systemic antibiotics as indicated
Treat dermatological causes, using topical or intralesional corticosteroids or immunotherapy for alopecia areata and managing cicatricial alopecias
Correct systemic contributors with thyroid hormone replacement for hypothyroidism, multidrug antimicrobial therapy for leprosy, and review of causative drugs
Address psychiatric causes such as trichotillomania with behavioural therapy and psychiatric support
Biopsy and refer any suspicious lid-margin lesion for management of possible eyelid malignancy
Cosmetic and restorative options including eyelash and eyebrow restoration, a prostaglandin-analogue eyelash agent, tattooing or grafting for permanent scarring loss
